name: MS Word Reading Locations
purpose: Records the last cursor/scroll position a user reached within a specific Word document, along with when that reading session ended, so Word can resume the document at the same spot next time it's opened.
key_fields: Position subkey values - per-document entries keyed by file path/identifier
Date - the last-closed timestamp for that reading session
Position - the stored location (page/character offset) within the document at close
normal_baseline: Entries for documents the user has recently read or edited, with Date values reasonably close to other evidence of Word being open, and positions scattered throughout each document consistent with normal reading/editing.
anomalies: A Reading Locations entry for a document with no corresponding File MRU or Trust Records entry, or vice versa, suggesting one artifact was cleared while the other was missed
A recorded closing position at or near the very start of a large document, inconsistent with a claim that the user reviewed its full contents
An entry for a document the user denies having opened, with a Date value falling inside a suspected incident window
A Reading Locations entry referencing a document path under a Temp, Downloads, or email-attachment cache directory rather than a normal working location
anti_forensic_notes: This key only tracks documents opened long or interactively enough for Word to record a reading position, so a document opened only briefly may leave no entry here even though it does elsewhere (File MRU, Trust Records). Deleting the key removes reading-position history without affecting the separate File MRU list, so the two should be checked independently rather than assumed to rise and fall together.
interpretation: Cross-referencing the Date (last-closed) value here against the last-opened time recorded in the corresponding Office File MRU entry for the same document lets an analyst calculate an approximate session duration - how long the user actually had the document open - which neither artifact provides on its own.
